content.text: Introduction

Managing multiple construction sites simultaneously is the daily routine for construction professionals. Between quotes, schedules, and invoices, Excel quickly becomes an inadequate tool. You waste precious time juggling spreadsheets, emails, and phone calls. What if you switched to a dedicated tool to gain efficiency and peace of mind?
Let's see together how an appropriate tool can transform your site management.
What it costs you

Using Excel to manage your construction sites is like trying to build a house with a hand drill. It might work for a small project, but as the workload increases, problems arise. You spend several hours a week updating spreadsheets, sending emails to confirm appointments, and searching for information lost in poorly organized files. Not to mention data entry errors that can cost time and money. Add to this the stress of not having a clear view of the progress of your construction sites, which can harm your relationship with your clients.
Why traditional solutions are not enough
Objection:
I have always used Excel, it works very well for me.
Response:

Excel is a versatile tool, but it is not designed to manage complex projects like construction sites. It lacks specific features to track the progress of work, manage teams and materials, and communicate effectively with clients. Moreover, it is difficult to collaborate in real-time with your employees and subcontractors, which can lead to delays and misunderstandings.
- Difficulty in tracking the progress of construction sites in real-time
- Risk of data entry errors and data loss
- Lack of real-time collaboration
- Difficulty in generating reports and invoices
The solution adapted to your profession

A tool dedicated to construction site management allows you to centralize all information in one place. You can track the progress of the work, manage teams and materials, and communicate easily with your clients. Additionally, you can automate certain tasks, such as generating quotes and invoices, saving you precious time. An adapted tool also allows you to delegate certain tasks to your employees more easily, allowing you to focus on what is really important: the quality of your construction sites.
Concrete example (detailed realistic case)

You are on a renovation site of several apartments, with several teams and subcontractors. You use a dedicated tool to manage schedules, tasks, and materials. You can see at a glance the progress of the work, potential delays, and problems to be solved. You communicate easily with your teams via the tool, avoiding misunderstandings and delays. You automatically generate quotes and invoices, saving you precious time. Your clients are informed in real-time of the progress of the work, which strengthens their confidence in you.

I start by analyzing your specific needs and your current work processes. Then, I propose a customized solution, adapted to your profession and your way of working. I accompany you in the implementation of the tool, the training of your teams, and the monitoring of the progress of the construction sites. I ensure that the tool meets your expectations and that you are satisfied with the result.

I help you identify your specific needs and choose the tool that best suits your profession and your way of working.
How to train my teams to use the tool?
I offer training adapted to your teams so that they can use the tool effectively and autonomously.

content.text: Why a management software is essential for plumbers

As a plumber, you know that managing your business can be complex. Between scheduling interventions, invoicing, inventory management, and customer relations, it's easy to get lost. This is where a management software tailored to your trade comes into play. By 2026, digital tools will be even more indispensable to stay competitive and provide flawless service to your customers.
SaaS vs Custom Solution: Key Differences
SaaS Software
A SaaS (Software as a Service) software is a cloud-hosted solution accessible via a web browser. Here are its main advantages:
Low initial cost
: No need to invest in hardware or servers.
Automatic updates
: You always benefit from the latest version without having to intervene.
Accessibility
: You can access it from any device connected to the Internet.
However, SaaS solutions also have drawbacks:
Limited customization
: You must adapt to the software, not the other way around.
Dependence on the provider
: You are at the mercy of the provider's decisions regarding pricing, features, etc.
Custom Solution
A custom solution is developed specifically to meet your needs. Here are its main advantages:
Full customization
: The software is designed to adapt to your business processes.
Data ownership
: You control your data and hosting.
Scalability
: You can add or modify features according to your needs.
The drawbacks of a custom solution are:
High initial cost
: Developing a custom software requires a larger investment.
Development time
: It takes time to design and deploy a custom solution.
How to choose between SaaS and a custom solution?
The choice between a SaaS software and a custom solution depends on several factors:
Your specific needs
: Do you have unique business processes that require a custom solution?
Your budget
: What is your initial and recurring budget for management software?
Your risk tolerance
: Are you willing to invest time and money in developing a custom solution?
Your technical skills
: Do you have the necessary skills to manage a custom solution?
My offer for plumbers

As a freelance developer based in Rennes, I offer custom solutions for tradespeople and SMEs. I can help you design a management software tailored to your specific needs, to optimize your business and provide flawless service to your customers.
Conclusion

The choice between a SaaS software and a custom solution depends on your needs, budget, and technical skills. If you have unique business processes or want full control over your data, a custom solution may be the best option. On the other hand, if you have a limited budget or prefer an off-the-shelf solution, a SaaS software may be more suitable.

blog/paysagiste-outil-metier-devis-chant.metaDescription: Recopied quotes, schedules disrupted by weather, wasted hours in the field: what a custom tool changes for a landscaper, without jargon.

content.text: I don’t trim hedges, and I’ve never laid a single border in my life. My job is to build tools for craftspeople, and to do that, I spend a lot of time watching people work. Among landscapers, there’s one object I see almost every time: an Excel spreadsheet. A big one. Opened in the evening, on the kitchen table, after a day outside. A spreadsheet that started simple and, over the seasons, has grown into a monster no one dares touch anymore.
This article is for you if you recognize yourself in this. Not to sell you a dream, but to show you, concretely, what you can do better.
Excel has served you well — until the day it starts holding you back

Let’s be honest: at first, Excel is great. It’s free or nearly free, almost everyone knows how to use it, and it does the job when you’re working alone with a few projects. The problem isn’t Excel. The problem is what you end up asking it to do.

You ask it to track your quotes, your schedule, your hours worked, your supplier list, your maintenance contracts, sometimes even your before-and-after photos pasted into a cell. But a spreadsheet wasn’t designed for that. So you improvise. You duplicate the “template” tab, rename the file “quote_MartinV2_final_really.xlsx,” end up with multiple versions of the same schedule, and one day a formula breaks without you knowing why, and a total comes out wrong.

The real warning sign isn’t complexity. It’s the moment when the spreadsheet lives on your office computer while you’re out on the job site, boots in the dirt, and you can’t check anything until tonight.
A landscaper’s quotes: where money is won or lost
Let’s look at the quote, because that’s often the most painful point.

A client calls, you go out, take measurements, jot them down in a notebook. In the evening, you open the quote from a past project that was similar, copy it, replace the lines, recalculate. You look up the current price of plants — the one from your last order at the nursery, not from another season. You adjust labor time based on gut feeling. And you cross your fingers you didn’t leave an old line that doesn’t belong there.

Once it’s sent, another problem arises: where is this quote? Accepted? Rejected? Waiting for a response for weeks? In Excel, this information doesn’t exist anywhere reliable. You keep it in your head, and your head is already full.

A custom tool changes that without magic. You start with a library of services that is yours: mowing, hedge trimming by the meter, creating flower beds, planting, with your up-to-date times and rates. You build a quote by assembling the blocks you know, on your phone, from the client’s garden if you want. And every quote has a clear status: sent, followed up, accepted. You can see at a glance what’s stalled and deserves a call.
Tracking jobs: did that one actually make you money?

Here’s a simple question many landscapers can’t answer precisely: on your last big job, did you make a profit? You estimated a certain number of days. In reality, it rained, the soil delivery was delayed, you had to come back on a Saturday. Where are the actual hours? In the notebook, in team text messages, in your memory. Nowhere in the same place. So you never really compare what was planned to what was done. And without that comparison, you keep recreating quotes that are a little too tight, season after season.

What a well-designed tool brings here isn’t surveillance. It’s memory. On each job, your crew logs their hours in two taps from the truck. Before-and-after photos are linked to the right client, not buried in your phone’s gallery. Ordered materials are listed. At the end, you see if the job lived up to its promises. Not to beat yourself up — to quote the next one with real numbers, your own numbers.

And those same details serve you beyond the field: when the accountant asks for receipts, when a client disputes an invoice, when you want to show off a successful project to a potential client. Everything is there, clean and retrievable.
The schedule: when the weather decides for you

A landscaper’s schedule is a living thing. It rains for days, and everything shifts. A creation job falls behind, and it eats into this week’s maintenance rounds. A client calls to move up their hedge trimming. On an Excel sheet, every change means manually moving cells, with the risk of forgetting to notify the right person.

And there’s this quirk of your trade that generic tools ignore: recurring maintenance. Mowing and hedge-trimming contracts that come back at regular intervals, for private clients and condos alike. In Excel, you manually carry them over, again and again, and a visit sometimes gets skipped without anyone noticing — until the client does.

A tool made for you knows the difference between a one-off job and maintenance that should automatically return to the schedule. It knows that next week, it’s time for a certain condo. It shows you where your teams are, which job can slide when the rain starts, and what absolutely must not slip through the cracks. You keep the decision. The tool just keeps track of everything you can no longer remember.
“Custom,” concretely, what does that change?

You might think there are already off-the-shelf software solutions for construction. That’s true. Sometimes they work perfectly, and in that case, I’ll tell you straight rather than trying to sell you something else.

But “custom” isn’t a luxury gimmick. It means a tool that speaks your language. That counts in linear meters of hedge and square meters of lawn, not in abstract references. That knows your services, your suppliers, your way of breaking down a season. That doesn’t force you to tick fifteen useless boxes designed for a plumber or a tiler. A tool that looks like your trade, not your neighbor’s.

And above all: a tool that builds on what already works in your organization, without breaking everything. The goal isn’t to turn you into an IT specialist. It’s to give you back your evenings and help you quote more accurately.
Your questions before getting started
Do I need to stop using Excel overnight?
No. We start from what you already have and move forward step by step — we begin with what’s costing you the most time today. Nothing breaks all at once.
Will it take me a long time to learn?
The goal is exactly the opposite: a simple tool, designed for your way of working, not for an IT specialist. If you need a thick manual to use it, we’ve made a mistake.
What if my business changes — a new hire, a new service, an expanded territory?
It’s designed to evolve with you. A custom tool grows with you; it’s not thrown away at the first change.
Are my data kept safe with me?
Yes. This is something we clarify from the start, even before writing the first line.
Can we look at your organization together?

If this article resonated with you, here’s what I propose, with no obligation. We take a moment — over the phone or around a coffee if you’re near Rennes — and you show me how you work today: your famous Excel file, your way of creating quotes, tracking jobs, and managing the schedule. From there, I’ll give you a clear, written action plan: what’s really holding you back, what’s worth automating first, what can stay as is, and where to start to get relief quickly. Not a technical tome — a document you understand and remain in control of, even if you later decide to do this with someone else, or not at all.
You know your trade better than anyone. My job is to make sure your tool stops holding you back and starts working for you.

blog/electricien-outil-sur-mesure-devis-.metaDescription: Late quotes, forgotten interventions at invoicing: a tool designed for your electrician trade brings order to your rounds. Let’s talk about it?

content.text: I don’t pull cables, and I’ve never opened an electrical panel in my life. But I’ve spent evenings sitting next to electricians who, once their last job was done, would sit down with a notebook and a phone full of site photos trying to remember what they had billed — and especially what they had forgotten.

If you’re a self-employed electrician or work with two or three guys, you know exactly what I’m talking about. During the day, you’re running around: a repair job in the morning, a renovation in the afternoon, a client calling at 7 p.m. because 'the circuit breaker tripped again.' And the paperwork? It waits until the evening. Or the weekend. Or never.
An electrician’s quote is almost always a race against time.

A private client calls you to redo their electrical panel. You go over, take measurements in your head, jot down a few things on a scrap of paper. Then you have to price it: materials, hours, compliance with regulations. Except you’re doing the quote in the evening, exhausted, between other tasks.

The result? It’s two days late. Sometimes three. And in the meantime, the client has called two other electricians. The one who answers first, neatly and with a clear quote, is often the one who lands the job — even if they’re not the cheapest.

The problem isn’t that you’re mispricing. It’s that putting together a quote drains all your energy when it should take ten minutes. Revisiting your rates, your usual material references, your presentation style — you’re doing it all from scratch every time.
The interventions you forget to bill

That’s where it really hurts. On a large, well-organized site, everything gets billed, no problem. The black hole is the small jobs: the one-hour repair, the extra socket 'while I’m at it,' the trip to a client’s neighbor.

You actually do those hours. But between the moment you close the panel and when you’re supposed to bill for them, a week passes, three other sites come up, and a good chunk of it vanishes. No one writes it down. No one claims it.

Ask yourself the real question: over the last month, how many hours did you actually work, and how many did you bill? If you can’t answer in three seconds, you’re probably losing several hundred euros a month — not because you’re doing bad work, but because nothing links 'I did the job' to 'I billed for it.'
Why 'all-in-one' management software ends up in the closet

So someone has probably already sold you a management software for tradespeople. You might even have paid for it. And it’s gathering dust somewhere because it takes twenty minutes of data entry for a one-hour repair, asks for fields that are irrelevant to your trade, and was never designed for an electrician working out of their van.
A tool that slows you down is one you won’t use. It’s that simple. And a tool you don’t use is worthless, even if it ticks every box on the brochure.
That’s the whole difference between generic software and a
custom tool
: the first forces you to adapt to its logic, the second fits yours. Your types of jobs, your usual materials, your way of billing travel time, your regular clients. Nothing more, nothing less.
A concrete example
Take Julien, an independent electrician with a van, sometimes an apprentice. Before, his management fit on a notebook, a spreadsheet, and his memory.

Now, he opens his phone on site. He creates the job in three clicks: the client, the address, what he did, the hours. The photo of the panel goes straight onto it. In the evening, there’s nothing left to 're-enter': everything he did that day is already there. All he has to do is turn each job into an invoice with a single gesture.

His recurring quotes — compliance checks, panels, light points — he pulls them from a template in two minutes, with his up-to-date rates. And once a week, he looks at one thing only: the jobs done but not yet billed. The list is short, and it no longer contains forgotten invoices worth €300.
Julien didn’t become an accountant. He just stopped leaving money on the table.
What does a custom tool for electricians look like, in practice?
Not a bloated system. A tool that does three or four things well — the ones that matter to you:
Enter a job in thirty seconds
, from the site, with photos.
See at a glance what hasn’t been billed yet
— the number one money leak.
Generate a clean quote in minutes
, based on your usual services and rates.
Access a client’s history
, when they call back six months later.
Everything else — accounting, stock, team scheduling — is added only if you really need it. We start from your daily reality, not a list of features.
In short
- A quote that’s sent quickly and neatly lands more jobs than a cheaper one that arrives late.
- The hours that slip away are the small jobs that go unbilled: that’s where the lost money is.
- Generic software that slows you down will end up in the closet; a tool tailored to your trade is one you’ll actually use.
- Don’t digitalize for the sake of digitalizing: first fix the pain point.
FAQ
Is a custom tool for electricians only for big companies?
No, it’s the opposite. A large company has a team for management. The solo electrician or a duo? They have no one — it’s precisely those for whom saving two hours a week changes everything.
I already have management software. Why change?

If you actually use it and it suits you, don’t change anything. If you paid for it but it’s gathering dust because it’s too cumbersome, the issue isn’t finding another one of the same kind — it’s having a tool you’ll actually open.
How much does a custom tool cost?

It depends on what you need, and honestly, sometimes an existing tool is enough — if that’s the case, I’ll tell you. The goal isn’t to sell you software; it’s to save you time and stop forgotten invoices.
How long does it take to set up?
We always start small: tackle the most painful point first (often unbilled jobs), get it up and running quickly, then add the rest as needed. No six-month mega-project.
Shall we talk?
If you recognized yourself in even one of these situations, we can take thirty minutes together. I’ll look at how you currently manage quotes, jobs, and invoices, and I’ll give you a
review of your organization
with a
written action plan
— the point where you’re losing the most money first, and a rough budget estimate.
And if an existing tool already does the job, I’ll tell you honestly.

blog/chauffagiste-contrats-entretien-out.title: Heating Engineer: Never Forget a Maintenance Visit Again
blog/chauffagiste-contrats-entretien-out.excerpt: Maintenance contracts stuck in a spreadsheet or just in your head mean lost revenue. Discover how a custom tool helps a heating engineer send reminders at the right time.
blog/chauffagiste-contrats-entretien-out.metaTitle: Heating Engineer: Managing Maintenance Contracts Without Missing a Thing
blog/chauffagiste-contrats-entretien-out.metaDescription: Annual visit reminders, boiler history, contract renewals: how a custom tool helps a heating engineer stay on top of everything.

content.text: I’m not a heating engineer. I’ve never bled a radiator or replaced a heat exchanger. But after building tools for tradespeople, I’ve seen the same scene play out time and again: a binder of maintenance contracts, a paper diary, and a spreadsheet where someone has scribbled 'Martin’s boiler — check in October.' Except it’s February, and no one’s called Martin.

Annual boiler servicing is the lifeblood of a heating engineer’s business: mandatory for the customer, recurring, and reliable revenue… as long as you don’t forget about it. And that’s exactly what happens when you try to manage it in your head or on the back of a spreadsheet.
The real problem for a heating engineer: recurrence, not the service itself

A heating engineer knows how to do their job. What trips them up isn’t the service call itself—it’s remembering—for 200, 300, or 400 clients—which ones are under contract, which boiler was installed when, and when the next visit is due.

When you do it by hand, two things always happen: either you follow up too late, and the customer has already gone to a competitor; or you forget entirely, and a missed visit means a contract that doesn’t get renewed. In both cases, it’s money slipping away without a sound.
What a custom tool changes in practice
The idea isn’t some bloated, all-singing, all-dancing software package. It’s a tool that answers three simple questions: who’s under contract, which visits are due, and have I followed up?
- Each customer has a profile with their boilers: brand, installation date, last service.
- The system automatically calculates upcoming visits and generates the month’s list.
- A reminder is sent automatically—via SMS or email—a few weeks before the due date.
Nothing flashy. Just the end of 'I must have forgotten someone.'
A concrete example

Take a heating engineer with 300 maintenance contracts. Every Monday morning, they open their tool: '14 visits to schedule this month, 3 customers not yet contacted.' They no longer open any spreadsheets. The relevant customers received an automatic reminder the previous week; all they have to do is schedule the appointments. By the end of the year, they can see at a glance how many contracts are up for renewal and which ones are at risk of lapsing. The time spent 'trying to remember who to call' drops to zero.
Boiler history: the detail that builds trust

Another game-changer: each boiler keeps its own history. When you return to a customer three years later, you know what’s been done, which parts were replaced, and you don’t have to rediscover the installation every time.
For the customer, it’s a pro who 'knows' their boiler. For the heating engineer, it means faster diagnostics, fewer surprises, and a rock-solid renewal argument.
Frequently asked questions
Does this replace my quotation and invoicing software?

Not necessarily. The tool can focus on what you’re missing—the contract tracking and follow-ups—and coexist with what you already use for billing. If an existing tool already does this well, I’ll tell you.
I have 400 customers in a spreadsheet—do I have to start from scratch?
No. We can import your spreadsheet to get the database started: you don’t have to re-enter 400 lines by hand.
Aren’t automatic reminders spam?
A service reminder—often mandatory and expected by the customer—isn’t spam. It’s a service they appreciate.
How long does it take to set up?
A first useful tool—customer profiles, upcoming visits, reminders—can be built in a few weeks, not six months.
Want to talk about it?

If your maintenance contracts live in a spreadsheet and in your head, we can start simply: an audit of your current setup and a written action plan. I always start with the pain point, give a rough budget estimate, and if an existing tool works for you, I’ll tell you.

Si vos contrats d'entretien vivent dans un tableur et dans votre tête, on peut commencer simplement : un audit de votre organisation actuelle et un plan d'action écrit. Je commence toujours par le point qui fait le plus mal, je donne un ordre de grandeur de budget honnête, et si un outil existant vous suffit, je vous le dis.

blog/serrurier-rennes-depannage-outil-su.metaDescription: Missed calls, intervention dispatch, quote follow-ups: how a custom tool helps a locksmith in Rennes avoid missing an emergency.

content.text: I'm not a locksmith. I've never picked a lock or installed a cylinder. But after working with craftsmen for so long, I've seen what happens when a locksmith is already on a job and the phone rings: either they answer and drop what they're doing, or they let it ring… and the next customer, the one locked out in Rennes on a Sunday evening, calls the competition.
For a locksmith, especially in emergency repairs, the real capital isn't the workshop. It's about
not missing a call
, and knowing at all times who is where and who is available. And a notebook and an answering machine are no longer enough.
The lifeblood of the trade: urgency, not the quote
A locksmith does two jobs in one: planned installations (doors, safes, access control) and
emergency repairs

(lockouts, break-ins, broken cylinders). The latter is unpredictable, highly competitive, and decided in minutes — especially in a city like Rennes, where the first to respond and arrive quickly wins the job.

The problem isn't knowing how to do the work. It's the orchestration: who takes the call, who is closest, who is free, and whether we’ve called back the customer from this morning who hasn’t had a response yet.
What a tailor-made tool changes
The idea isn’t a giant management software. It’s a tool designed for urgency:
Every call is logged
— even the ones we couldn’t answer — so we can call back immediately instead of forgetting about them.
Today’s jobs
are visible at a glance: who, where, at what time.
Installation quotes
are sent and followed up automatically, so non-urgent requests don’t slip through the cracks.
The goal: no call, no quote falls through the cracks.
A concrete example

A locksmith in Rennes and its outskirts, with two technicians on the road. A call comes in during a job: instead of losing it, it’s logged in two seconds, and the other technician immediately sees “door opening, Cesson-Sévigné, in 20 minutes.” By evening, the list of unprocessed requests is empty — not by luck, but because nothing was forgotten. And the installation quotes sent last week were automatically followed up: two turned into jobs.
Location matters

For emergency repairs, proximity is everything. A tool that knows where each job is allows us to send the right technician to the right place — and tell the customer “we’ll be there in 20 minutes” with confidence. In Rennes, between the city center, the ring road, and the surrounding towns, that’s often what wins the job.
Frequently asked questions
I work alone. Is it worth it?
Yes, maybe even more so: when you’re on your own, every missed call is a lost job. A tool that logs requests and follows up on quotes is revenue you’re no longer letting slip away.
I already have invoicing software.
You don’t necessarily need to replace it. The tool can focus on what’s missing — tracking calls and jobs — and coexist with the rest.
Does it work on the phone, in the field?
That’s actually the starting point: a locksmith spends their day outside. The tool needs to be usable one-handed, in the van, not just in the office.
Starting from scratch?
No. We retrieve what you already have — customers, quotes — so you don’t have to re-enter everything.
Want to talk about it?

If your calls and quotes are still in a notebook and your memory, we can start simply: an audit of your organization and a written action plan. I’ll start with the point that hurts the most, give you an honest budget, and if an existing tool works for you, I’ll tell you so.

blog/developpeur-application-metier-renn.title: Business application developer in Rennes: why proximity makes all the difference
blog/developpeur-application-metier-renn.excerpt: Entrusting your custom business tool to a freelance developer near Rennes: what proximity really changes, with a concrete case and an honest budget.
blog/developpeur-application-metier-renn.metaTitle: Custom business application developer in Rennes | Dibodev
blog/developpeur-application-metier-renn.metaDescription: A custom business tool developed by a freelance developer near Rennes: what proximity changes for a small or medium-sized business, with a concrete example and a clear budget.

content.text: Three weeks ago, I stopped by to see the manager of a small maintenance company, about twenty minutes from Rennes. Eight employees, a full order book, and on his desk: two screens on… and a spiral-bound notebook placed between them. The week’s interventions were written in the notebook in pen. 'The software doesn’t do it the way I want,' he told me, shrugging. So he doubles everything: once in the SaaS they sold him, once in the notebook 'to be sure.'
This manager doesn’t have a motivation problem. He has a tool problem. And that’s exactly where a business application developer can change his week—especially when they’re just around the corner.
A business tool isn’t just another piece of software

When I talk about custom business applications, people often imagine a big, expensive project reserved for large companies. In reality, it’s the opposite. It’s a tool tailored to your way of working: yours. Not thirty features you only use three of, but the three that waste two hours of your day—done right.

For this maintenance manager, the real issue wasn’t 'I need software.' It was: 'I want to see, every Monday morning, who’s going where during the week, and know at a glance what hasn’t been invoiced.' No generic SaaS checked those boxes without forcing him to twist his workflow to fit their mold. A custom tool, on the other hand, starts with his notebook—not a template designed for a business that isn’t his.
Why 'near Rennes' makes a difference
You might think a developer can be managed remotely from anywhere. That’s true on paper. But a business tool isn’t built by reading a requirements document: it’s built by watching someone work.

Being on-site around Rennes means I can sit in your office for an hour, watch that infamous Excel file open for real, and hear the 'oh yeah, but we never do it like that.' Those little details are what make the difference between a tool people adopt and one they abandon after a month.
Proximity, in concrete terms, gives three things:
- We meet in person.
A kickoff meeting at your table is worth ten video calls. You show me, I understand the ground reality, and we don’t waste three weeks on misunderstandings.
- Responsiveness.
A bug on Tuesday morning, a 'hey, we should add this'—I’m in the same time zone, the same week, reachable—no offshore hotline with ticket number 4712.
- No black box.
You know who’s coding your tool; you can make me coffee while showing me the problem. It might seem trivial, but it’s what makes a project succeed.

The Rennes metropolitan area is a fabric of SMEs and micro-enterprises running on jury-rigged tools because custom solutions have long seemed out of reach. A local freelancer is precisely the way to get one without the cost or bureaucracy of an agency.
A concrete example: Monday morning the week before

Let’s go back to the maintenance company. Today, their Monday morning looks like this: they open their schedule in a software, copy the interventions into the notebook, call two technicians to confirm, and realize on Thursday that three interventions from the previous week were never invoiced. Multiply that by a year: that’s thousands of euros slipping through the cracks—not out of malice, just friction.

A custom tool here could fit on three screens: the week’s schedule showing who’s going where, an intervention sheet a technician fills out from their phone after leaving the site, and an 'unbilled' list that updates automatically as soon as an intervention is marked complete. Nothing flashy. Just the end of the notebook—and the end of forgotten invoices.
This isn’t science fiction or a six-month project. It’s the kind of tool you scope in one meeting and deliver in small pieces, starting with what hurts the most.
‘How much does it cost?’—the real question

Let’s be direct, because it’s the question everyone asks without daring to: yes, developing a custom tool represents a budget. But the right comparison isn’t 'custom vs. free.' It’s 'the cost of the tool vs. the cost of your current workflow'—the hours spent copying, the forgotten invoices, the errors you have to fix.

My approach boils down to three points. We start with the problem that hurts the most, not a bloated system. I give you a honest ballpark estimate from the first conversation, not a vague quote. And if, after listening to you, I realize an existing software would work just as well for much less, I’ll tell you—I’d rather have a client who comes back than a forced sale.
FAQ
Do you need to be a large company for a custom tool?

No, quite the opposite. SMEs and micro-enterprises are the ones who benefit the most from automating the two or three tasks eating up their days. We size the tool to the need, not the other way around.
How long before I have something usable?
We deliver in stages. A first version that solves the most painful problem can be up and running in a few weeks, then we expand based on real-world feedback.
I’m in Vitré, Bruz, Cesson… does it still work?
Yes. I work with companies across the entire Rennes metropolitan area and Brittany. Proximity is a plus, not a boundary—we always find the right balance between on-site meetings and remote follow-up.
What if I already have software I don’t like?
We first look at whether we can improve it or connect it to a small complementary tool before starting from scratch. Starting over is never the first option I propose.

If you recognize yourself in the manager with the spiral notebook, the simplest thing is to talk about it. I always start with an audit of your workflow and a written action plan—you leave with something useful, even if we don’t end up working together.

Faut-il être une grosse entreprise pour un outil sur mesure ?
Non, au contraire. Les TPE et PME sont celles qui gagnent le plus à automatiser les deux ou trois tâches qui grignotent leurs journées. On dimensionne l'outil au besoin, pas l'inverse.
Combien de temps avant d'avoir quelque chose d'utilisable ?
On livre par étapes. Une première version qui règle le problème le plus douloureux peut être en service en quelques semaines, puis on enrichit selon les retours du terrain.
Je suis à Vitré, Bruz, Cesson… ça marche aussi ?

Oui. Je travaille avec des entreprises de tout le bassin rennais et de Bretagne. La proximité est un plus, pas une frontière — on trouve toujours le bon mélange entre rendez-vous sur place et suivi à distance.
Et si j'ai déjà un logiciel que je n'aime pas ?
On regarde d'abord si on peut l'améliorer ou le connecter à un petit outil complémentaire avant de tout refaire. Repartir de zéro n'est jamais la première option que je propose.

Si vous vous reconnaissez dans le gérant au cahier à spirales, le plus simple est d'en parler. Je commence toujours par un audit de votre organisation et un plan d'action écrit — vous repartez avec quelque chose d'utile, même si on ne travaille pas ensemble ensuite.

blog/logiciel-metier-b2b-quitter-excel-s.title: B2B Business Software: 5 Signs It's Time to Move Beyond Excel
blog/logiciel-metier-b2b-quitter-excel-s.excerpt: When shared Excel files become more of a risk than a tool: 5 concrete signs that a B2B SME should transition to a custom business software solution.
blog/logiciel-metier-b2b-quitter-excel-s.metaTitle: Developing B2B Business Software: Moving Beyond Excel | Dibodev
blog/logiciel-metier-b2b-quitter-excel-s.metaDescription: Spreadsheets multiplying, errors, scattered data: 5 signs that a B2B SME needs custom business software, and how to make the switch.

content.text: In almost every B2B SME I step into, there’s a single file. One file. It’s called something like `client_tracking_2024_V3_FINAL(really).xlsx`, it weighs fifteen tabs, and only one person truly knows how it works. The day she’s on vacation, the entire department holds its breath.

Excel is great. It’s often the right choice to start with: free, flexible, and everyone knows how to use it. The problem isn’t Excel—it’s the moment when your business has outgrown it without anyone noticing. Here are five signs I hear in meetings that all mean the same thing: it’s time to switch to a real business software.
1. Multiple people need to edit the same file at the same time

This is the classic scenario. Two salespeople open the tracking file, each on their own end, and by evening, someone has to 'merge' it—meaning one person manually copies the other’s entries, hoping nothing is missed. Or the file is on a shared drive, and you start seeing copies labeled `- Copy`, `- Julie’s edits`, `- do not use`.

An Excel file was never meant to serve as a multi-user database. The moment multiple hands are writing in it, you’re no longer working with data—you’re managing versions. A business software, on the other hand, assumes ten people can write simultaneously, and the data remains single and unified.
2. You spend more time correcting than producing

A client billed twice. An order processed incorrectly because it was on the wrong tab. A total that doesn’t add up, and no one knows why. If your team spends Friday afternoons 'making sure everything is correct,' it’s not a matter of rigor—it’s a structural issue.

Excel lets you write anything, even nonsense. A tailored tool puts safeguards where they matter: you can’t validate an order without a client, you can’t bill the same service twice, a status can’t be both 'paid' and 'pending.' These small, invisible constraints eliminate errors at the source.
3. 'That? It’s in Marc’s file.'

When I ask where a specific piece of information is, and the answer is 'Oh, that’s Marc’s responsibility—it’s in his file,' I know the company operates in silos. Sales tracking here, production there, invoicing in a third spreadsheet, with copy-pasting and emails with attachments bridging the gaps.

The cost of these silos is invisible but real: no one has a full picture, the same data is entered three times, and when Marc leaves, part of the company’s memory walks out with him. A business software brings these pieces together in one place, where everyone sees what concerns them without having to ask.
4. There’s a formula no one dares touch
In every large Excel file, there’s
the

cell. A sprawling formula written three years ago by someone who may no longer be there, on which everything else depends. No one truly understands it, so no one touches it—people build on top of it, crossing their fingers.

This is technical debt, just like in software, except it’s hidden in a spreadsheet. When it breaks, it breaks everything. When a company reaches this point, it’s the clearest sign that its tool has become more fragile than its business can afford.
5. You can’t answer a simple question in ten seconds

'How much have we billed this client since January?' 'Which orders are overdue?' 'What did each salesperson close this quarter?' If the answer to these questions is 'Give me an hour—I’ll make a pivot table,' you don’t have a management tool—you have an archive.

A B2B business software is first and foremost this: being able to ask a question about your business and get the answer immediately. Not once a month when someone has time to compile it, but on demand, up to date, for everyone.
Making the leap without breaking everything
The good news is you don’t need to replace ten years of Excel in a weekend—and you don’t have to. My approach is simple: start with
the file that hurts the most
, the one everything else depends on, and replace it with a tool that does exactly what it did—only better, safer, and multi-user. The rest follows in stages, once trust is established.
I always give an
honest ballpark budget estimate
from the very first conversation, and I stick to one rule:
if your Excel still does the job, I’ll tell you so.
Switching to a business software should save you time and peace of mind—not saddle you with a project you don’t need.
FAQ
Does a custom software solution only suit large companies?
No. B2B SMEs are often the ones suffering the most from Excel’s limitations because they’ve grown faster than their tools. We size the software to your real needs, not your company’s size.
How long does it take to replace our main file?
A first version that takes over the role of your most critical file can be up and running in a few weeks. We then move forward in small increments, never disrupting operations.
Will we lose our Excel data during migration?
No—quite the opposite. We start from your existing files to initialize the software. Your history is preserved, not discarded.
What if we just want to better organize our files, not switch to a software?
That’s a valid option, and I’ll tell you if that’s the case. Sometimes, a few automations are enough before considering a full development.

blog/freelance-ou-agence-rennes-outil-me.title: Freelance or Agency in Rennes: Which to Choose for Your Business Tool?
blog/freelance-ou-agence-rennes-outil-me.excerpt: Freelance or agency in Rennes for your custom software? A local developer honestly compares the two and explains when each option is the right choice.
blog/freelance-ou-agence-rennes-outil-me.metaTitle: Freelance or Agency in Rennes for Your Business Tool | Dibodev
blog/freelance-ou-agence-rennes-outil-me.metaDescription: Freelance or web agency in Rennes to develop a custom business tool? The real criteria for SMEs, without any fluff.

content.text: "We asked three providers, and the quotes range from one to four times the price." This is a phrase I often hear when a company in Rennes contacts me about a custom tool. Between the web agency in the city center, the Parisian provider who responds by email, and the freelancer they were recommended, it's hard to know who does what—and above all, who is suited to their needs.

Let me be upfront: I’m a freelance developer near Rennes myself, so I’m not neutral. But I’ll still be honest because in some cases, an agency is genuinely the right choice. Here’s how I see things when a small or medium-sized business hesitates between the two for their business software.
What you’re really paying for at an agency

An agency is a team: a project manager, one or two developers, sometimes a designer, a salesperson. This structure has real advantages—multiple people on your project, continuity if someone leaves, the ability to handle large volumes. But it comes at a cost, and you pay that cost whether you need it or not.

Concretely, for a small business’s business tool, part of the agency’s bill goes toward internal coordination meetings, layers of intermediaries, and structural overhead. It’s not theft—it’s the price of an organization. The question to ask is simple: Does your project need this organization, or are you paying for an oversized machine to meet a need that fits on three screens?
What a freelancer changes—for better and for worse

With a freelancer, you speak directly to the person who will code. No intermediaries, no Chinese whispers between your needs and the result. You explain once to someone who will execute, not to a project manager who will "pass it up." For a business tool where the devil is in the details, this is often what makes the difference between a tool that fits and one that misses the mark.
The rate is usually lower because there’s no structure to fund. And responsiveness is better: one person, one point of contact, one to-do list.

But let’s be honest about the limitations. A freelancer is just one person: if they’re sick or overwhelmed, there’s no team to take over immediately. You need to choose someone reliable, set clear boundaries, and ensure the code belongs to you and remains maintainable if you ever change providers. A good freelancer will bring this up themselves; be wary of those who dodge the question.
The real criterion: the nature of your project
Forget the question "freelance or agency" for a moment and ask yourself the real one:
what does my project need?
An
agency

is often the right choice if you’re launching a large platform with multiple functions, if you need a contractual 24/7 support guarantee, or if the project will require several developers working in parallel for months.
A
freelance

is often the right choice for a targeted business tool: automating a specific process, replacing an unmanageable Excel file, connecting two software systems that don’t communicate, or digitizing a tracking system that’s costing you hours. In other words… the vast majority of needs for a small or medium-sized business.

If you’re still unsure, here’s a good indicator: Can you describe your need in one clear sentence? If yes, a freelancer will likely get it done faster and cheaper. If your need is vague and sprawling, a scoping phase—which I also offer—is better than rushing to the biggest provider.
In Rennes, concretely

The advantage of a local provider, whether agency or freelancer, is that you can meet in person. And for a business tool, meeting in person changes everything: I come sit in your workspace, I watch how you actually work, I see the overflowing spreadsheet. A ten-page specification will never replace an hour spent beside you.

Rennes has a dense tech ecosystem, with good freelancers and good agencies. You have a choice—take advantage of it by meeting both types before deciding. A simple coffee will tell you more about the person building your tool than three PDF quotes.
FAQ
Isn’t a freelancer risky if I depend on one person?

It’s a valid concern. We manage this by setting clear terms: documented code, hosting in your name, guaranteed ownership of the code. The goal is to ensure you’re never trapped by your provider, freelance or agency.
Isn’t an agency more "serious"?
Not necessarily. Seriousness comes from method and relationship, not size. Many small businesses in Rennes have worked successfully with freelancers for years.
Roughly how much price difference is there?

It depends on the project, but for a small business’s business tool, the gap between a freelancer and an agency is often significant at comparable quality—precisely because there’s no structure to fund.
Can I work with your current agency?
Yes, it happens: stepping in to reinforce a specific area or taking over a project cleanly. We’ll look together at what makes sense for you.

If you’re unsure about your own project, the simplest thing is to talk about it. I always start with an audit of your needs and a written action plan—and if I think an agency would be better suited to your case, I’ll tell you honestly.

blog/logiciel-gestion-auto-ecole-plannin.title: Driving school management software: ending the era of the wall planner
blog/logiciel-gestion-auto-ecole-plannin.excerpt: Scheduling, student tracking, hours, payments: how custom software helps a driving school move beyond the wall planner and binders, with a real-world case study.
blog/logiciel-gestion-auto-ecole-plannin.metaTitle: Custom driving school management software | Dibodev
blog/logiciel-gestion-auto-ecole-plannin.metaDescription: Instructor scheduling, student tracking, hours, and payments: why custom software transforms the operations of a driving school. With a real-world example.

content.text: The first time I looked inside a driving school from the inside, what struck me wasn’t the driving—it was the wall. A large erasable schedule, instructors in columns, time slots in rows, and scribbles everywhere: a student shifted, an instructor is sick, a car is in the garage. Next to it, a binder per student and a notebook for hours. Everything fit in the manager’s head, and the day she took an afternoon off, no one knew who was supposed to drive with whom.

A driving school isn’t a complicated business. But it is a business with a lot of small, moving parts—dozens of students, several instructors, hours to track, payments spread out—and it’s exactly these small, moving parts that a custom software effortlessly absorbs.
The schedule: the real headache

A driving school’s schedule is in constant flux. A student cancels the day before, a time slot opens up, an instructor combines theory and driving lessons, a car needs to go in for inspection. On a wall schedule or a shared spreadsheet, every change triggers three more, and one oversight is enough for a student to show up at a closed door or two students to be assigned to the same car.

A tool designed for a driving school starts from this reality: at a glance, you see who is driving, with which instructor, in which car, and a freed-up time slot is automatically reproposed. The schedule stops being a source of anxiety and becomes a simple reflection of the day.
Tracking students: where is everyone at?

‘How many hours does he have left?’ In many driving schools, the answer is in a binder or in the memory of the instructor who follows him. As long as everything goes well, it’s fine. The problem arises when you need to decide who to present for the exam, follow up with a student who is falling behind, or justify a remaining balance to a parent who asks questions.

A specialized software keeps each student’s package, hours completed, progress, and documents in one place. Anyone in the driving school can answer in ten seconds without digging. And the student, for his part, feels supported—which matters more than you’d think for word-of-mouth referrals.
Hours and payments: where money gets lost

This is the most sensitive—and quietest—point. Hours completed but never invoiced. A package paid in three installments that gets lost in the shuffle. A student who ‘already paid,’ and no one remembers. Over a year, it’s not just a few euros: it’s a real share of the turnover that evaporates, without anyone having done anything wrong.

A custom tool links hours, packages, and payments: as soon as a lesson is completed, it’s deducted; as soon as a balance is due, it’s visible. You stop searching, and above all, you stop losing money.
A tool tailored for a driving school, not a generic calendar

There are calendars and off-the-shelf software. Some work perfectly well at first—and if one of them is enough for your driving school, I’ll tell you so honestly. But many managers end up twisting them to fit their needs: a field repurposed here, a spreadsheet alongside there, and you’re back to double the work.

Custom software does the opposite: it starts from your way of working—your packages, your rules, your organization—and fits it exactly. No thirty useless features, just yours, done right. And it’s built in stages, starting with what’s costing you the most time today.
FAQ
Is it worth it for a small driving school?
Yes, often even more so. Small businesses suffer the most from repetitive tasks because the manager does everything. Automating the schedule and tracking hours frees up precious time.
How long before the tool is usable?
We start with the most painful point—often the schedule or tracking hours—and a first version can be up and running in a few weeks, then we build on it.
Can we import our current data?
Yes. We start from your existing files and binders to initialize the tool: nothing is lost, everything is carried over.
What about the online theory test part?
We can either connect to it or leave it as is. The idea isn’t to replace everything, but to make the manual work around it disappear.

If you recognize yourself in the wall schedule full of scribbles, the simplest thing is to talk about it. I always start with an audit of your organization and a written action plan—you leave with something useful, even if we don’t work together afterward.
